findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation deferral announced early September 2026; unitary council to begin March 2028, reducing immediate uncertainty but structural change confirmed
findings.detail: LGR will end Tonbridge and Malling in March 2028. Recent deferral announcement in early September 2026 has reduced immediate uncertainty. Risk of operational shortfall from staff departures persists. New unitary council may be burdened with historic county debt. Shared strategic partner being procured to support collaboration through Vesting Day April 2028. Close working at Leader and Chief Executive level. Risk score 16.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has leadership stability through 2028, whether debt obligations are being managed, and what structural changes will affect successor council creditworthiness
findings.figures: Vesting Day April 2028; LGR deferral announced early September 2026; risk score 16
findings.quote: Recent announcement on deferal of LGR in early September 2026 has resulted in longer term risk being reduced

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Managed exit from Agile system and transition back to Uniform — new operational risk with data transfer and staffing implications
findings.detail: Council executing managed exit from Agile system with return to Uniform system. PID signed with IDOX establishing technical requirements for data return. Clear project plan with achievable milestones. Post-implementation review being carried out by internal audit with live lessons learned being implemented. Continued monitoring by implementation staff. Risk identified September 2026. Risk score 12.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's planning and regulatory systems remain stable during this transition and whether there are risks to data integrity
findings.figures: Risk identified September 2026; risk score 12; PID signed with IDOX
findings.quote: Failure to deliver a managed exit from Agile and transition back to Uniform System

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Staff recruitment and retention pressures addressed with 4% pay award agreed February 2026
findings.detail: Loss of capacity due to staff retirements (workforce age profile), staff departures to higher-paying roles, recruitment difficulties in key professional roles, and uncertainty from Local Government Reorganisation. Competition from private sector and London Boroughs. Council agreed 4% pay award in February 2026. Workforce Strategy reviewed June 2026. Market Supplement Policy in use for difficult-to-resource roles. Risk score 16 unmitigated, 12 mitigated.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can maintain service delivery and financial control with stable staffing, and whether pay inflation is sustainable
findings.figures: 4% pay award February 2026; Workforce Strategy reviewed June 2026; risk score 16 unmitigated, 12 mitigated
findings.quote: Pay award of 4% agreed by Council in February 2026 has helped in ensuring that pay remains competitive with others in the County and therefore score has been reduced.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs rising significantly; council deploying £1.6m Local Authority Housing Fund to develop council-owned accommodation portfolio
findings.detail: Housing need creating sustained increase in temporary accommodation costs. Council received £1.6m Local Authority Housing Fund and is developing council-owned/leased accommodation portfolio, implementing downsizing policy for larger properties, and working with housing providers on homelessness prevention. Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy 2026–2031 under development. Risk score 20 unmitigated, 12 mitigated.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council is managing homelessness cost pressures sustainably and whether external funding is being deployed effectively
findings.figures: £1.6m Local Authority Housing Fund; risk score 20 unmitigated, 12 mitigated
findings.quote: Development of council owned/leased temporary accommodation portfolio - including delivery of the Local Authority Housing Fund £1.6m funding received.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Development Management decisions blocked by insufficient infrastructure capacity — identified March 2026, unresolved at September review
findings.detail: The council is unable to make a full range of planning decisions due to evidence of insufficient infrastructure capacity, backing up planning decisions in the system. Statutory provider discussions ongoing. Precautionary approach adopted where all DM decisions reviewed for material considerations. Developers requested to provide individual infrastructure requirements for major applications. Risk score 20 unmitigated, reduced to 8 with mitigation.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can process development and generate planning fees as planned, and whether infrastructure investment is proceeding as required
findings.figures: Risk identified March 2026; score 20 unmitigated, 8 mitigated
findings.quote: Being unable to make a full range of Planning decisions due to evidence of insufficient infrastructure capacity would result in planning decisions being held up and backed up in the system.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Government intervention in planning process after council voted to pause Local Plan on 3 September 2026

MHCLG intervened the following day directing the council to progress with Reg 19 consultation, plan submission and examination. findings.matters: Finance directors track declining interest income closely; it could reflect falling deposit balances (consumed by capital expenditure) or lower projected interest rates, both affecting the revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: Major capital projects with borrowing implications coming; audit recommends enhanced reporting on affordability and funding
findings.detail: For the second consecutive year, Grant Thornton identified no significant weaknesses in the council's financial sustainability or governance. findings.matters: Lenders need to understand planned capital projects, their total costs, how they will be funded and what borrowing is required. An audit recommendation for enhanced reporting suggests these details are not currently fully transparent.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: Investment performance of 3.93% as at 30 June 2026 is in-line with the local authority benchmark average of 3.98%.
findings.detail: Benchmarking data from MUFG shows the council achieved 3.93% return as at 30 June 2026, matching the local authority peer group average. The council's risk exposure also remains consistent with local authority average, indicating appropriate calibration of risk to the Treasury Code's priority hierarchy of security, liquidity, then yield.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council is achieving competitive returns without excessive risk-taking; confirms investment strategy is appropriately positioned against peer councils.
findings.figures: Council return 3.93% as at 30 June 2026; local authority benchmark average 3.98%
findings.quote: As at 30 June 2026, the Council's return was 3.93% (purple diamond) in-line with the local benchmarking group average of 3.98%.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: Bank Rate is forecast to remain at 3.75% through 2026 then decline to 3.25% by March 2028.
findings.detail: MUFG's August 2026 forecasts predict Bank Rate will hold at 3.75% for the next four quarters (through June 2027), then decline to 3.50% by September 2027 and settle at 3.25% from December 2027. This is a slight upward revision from previous forecasts but remains broadly consistent with January 2026 assumptions. Declining rates will reduce future investment returns as maturing funds are reinvested at lower rates.
findings.matters: Finance directors use interest rate forecasts to budget investment income; the forecast decline signals that the council's current £780k annual interest earnings are unlikely to persist and will shrink progressively.
findings.figures: Bank Rate forecast: 3.75% through June 2027; 3.50% by September 2027; 3.25% December 2027 onwards
findings.quote: In the short term, the forecast Bank Rate has revised slightly upward to reflect current market conditions, with rates expected to remain at 3.75% for the next four quarters. Over the longer term, rates are forecast to gradually realign, with the Bank Rate expected to settle at 3.25% by March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: The council undertook no borrowing in the first four months of 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council has managed entirely from existing cash reserves and operational cash flows, with no resort to borrowing or PWLB funding. With average cash flow surpluses of £21.56m and core cash balances of £36m, the council invested £63.81m across money market funds, fixed deposits, property funds and multi-asset funds, eliminating immediate external financing needs.
findings.matters: Indicates a sound liquidity position and financial stability with no pressure to access debt markets; relevant to creditworthiness assessment and near-term financing risk.
findings.figures: Total funds invested £63.81m; cash flow surpluses £21.56m average; core cash balances £36m
findings.quote: No borrowing was undertaken during April to July 2026.

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: The council's £2m property fund investment has depreciated significantly, with capital value down £267,750 as at 31 July 2026.
findings.detail: The CCLA Local Authority Property Fund, originally invested at £2m, stood at £1,732,250 on 31 July 2026. The paper acknowledges that higher-yielding investments fluctuate in value and capital values may fall significantly during economic downturns; the investment's duration risk means losses could persist if the fund were sold in the near term. Cumulative dividend income of £699,430 has substantially offset the capital loss, yielding a net benefit of £431,680 since inception.
findings.matters: Signals illiquidity and mark-to-market exposure in the portfolio; lenders and finance directors need visibility of downside risk in longer-term investments and understand that higher yields carry depreciation risk.
findings.figures: Purchase price £2,000,000; sale value 31 July 2026 £1,732,250; total change in principal (267,750); cumulative dividends £699,430; net benefit since inception £431,680

findings.paper_title: Report of Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer
findings.headline: The council earned £172,050 more interest on its cash balances than budgeted in the first four months of 2026/27.
findings.detail: Interest earned from surplus cash flow and core cash balances totalled £780,050 by end July, outperforming the original estimate by £172,050. findings.matters: The favourable variance indicates the council's budget assumptions were conservative, providing more funding headroom than planned; it also demonstrates effective cash management responding to interest rate conditions.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Strategic Risk Register - Red risks
findings.headline: Central government directed the council to continue Local Plan making on 4 September 2026 after the council voted to pause it.
findings.detail: The council identified that infrastructure providers cannot meet service delivery timescales required by the Local Plan and voted to pause plan-making on 3 September 2026. MHCLG intervened and directed the council to proceed with plan making, examination and submission. The council submitted a formal response to the Minister on 11 September 2026 explaining the exceptional circumstances but is proceeding under government direction.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether councils can be forced to proceed with strategic commitments despite identified constraints on their delivery partners.

findings.quote: MHCLG wrote to the Council on 4 September 2026 to intervene in the process and direct the Council to progress with Plan making through Reg 19 consultation, Plan submission and examination.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Grant Thornton Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: Government paused local government reorganisation decisions in September 2026 that would have affected the council, creating governance and financial stewardship risks for 2026-27.
findings.detail: The council submitted a Strategic Business Case in November 2025 as part of Local Government Reorganisation proposals. The government announced its preferred option for Kent LGR (four unitary councils, no boundary changes) in July 2026. However, on 7 September 2026 the government announced a pause to LGR decisions and is reviewing the Kent decision. The auditors identify that heightened risks remain during 2026-27 including ensuring appropriate financial stewardship and governance are maintained, managing potential disaggregation and aggregation of services and finances, and ensuring appropriate resources are in place to deliver 2026-27 and 2027-28 accounts.
findings.matters: Organisational restructuring creates significant operational and financial transition risk; lenders need assurance that a council can maintain effective financial controls, governance, and service delivery continuity through an uncertain reorganisation period, and that management has capacity to handle both business-as-usual and transition activities.
findings.figures: LGR decision announced 7 September 2026 as paused; vesting date for new unitaries unconfirmed; Shadow Authority elections (originally May 2027) now to be held on existing council boundaries
findings.quote: On 7 September 2026 the government announced a pause to LGR decisions. The decisions relating to Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk and Hampshire (originally announced on 26 March 2026) have been withdrawn. For other LGR geographies, the government's decisions announced on 16 July 2026 are paused and are to be reviewed.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Grant Thornton Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: Auditors identified no significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements and expect to issue an unqualified opinion on the financial statements, though three improvement recommendations were raised.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton completed audit testing and intends to issue an unqualified audit opinion on the council's 2025-26 financial statements, confirming that the financial statements give a true and fair view and have been properly prepared in accordance with the CIPFA Code. Across all three value for money assessment areas (financial sustainability, governance, and efficiency), the auditors identified no significant weaknesses. The auditors did not issue any statutory recommendations, make applications for judicial review, or issue a Public Interest Report. Three improvement recommendations were raised but these relate to reporting enhancements rather than control deficiencies.
findings.matters: Lenders use audit qualifications and significant weakness findings as indicators of control environment; absence of qualifications and significant weaknesses provides baseline assurance on financial reporting reliability and governance effectiveness.
findings.figures: Zero significant weaknesses identified; three improvement recommendations; zero statutory recommendations; zero Public Interest Reports
findings.quote: We intend to issued an unqualified opinion on the Council's financial statements following the Audit Committee meeting on 28 September 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Grant Thornton Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: The Angel Centre capital project, the council's largest planned capital investment at £19.4m, may require borrowing but financing strategy and affordability analysis remain incomplete.
findings.detail: The Angel Centre is the council's largest planned capital investment with total estimated cost of £19.4m, with £15.0m profiled in 2026-27. Financing options remain under development and borrowing may be required during the project lifecycle. The revenue consequences of future borrowing are not yet fully reflected in the MTFS, meaning Members lack full visibility over borrowing requirements, impact on reserves, and affordability implications. The auditors raised an improvement recommendation requiring management to strengthen Member reporting on funding strategy, borrowing requirements and impact on the MTFS.
findings.matters: A capital project of this scale requiring potential new borrowing represents a material change to the council's debt position and affordability; lenders need understanding of how £19.4m will be funded, what borrowing is required, and whether repayment is affordable within Medium-Term Financial Strategy assumptions.
findings.figures: £19.4m total estimated cost; £15.0m profiled in 2026-27
findings.quote: Key finding: The Angel Centre construction project is the Council's largest planned capital investment, with total estimated cost of £19.4m (£15.0m profiled in 2026-27). Financing options remain under development, and borrowing may be required during the project life-cycle.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Grant Thornton Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: Council has eliminated its previously-forecast £2.8m medium-term funding gap and now forecasts a balanced budget with planned reserve contributions rather than depletion.
findings.detail: In prior years the MTFS identified a potential funding gap of £2.8m. Following the Local Government Finance Settlement and updated financial assumptions in 2026, management has demonstrated this gap is eliminated. The 2026-27 budget is approved as balanced and the council no longer forecasts a funding gap over the planning period. The council has moved from reliance on reserve depletion to planned reserve contributions, demonstrating improved medium-term financial resilience.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can sustain services without structural deficits requiring reserves depletion; movement from a £2.8m forecast gap to a balanced position with reserve rebuilding indicates improved debt sustainability and reduced default risk.
findings.figures: £2.8m funding gap eliminated; 2026-27 budget approved as balanced; planned contributions to reserves rather than reliance on reserve depletion
findings.quote: management has demonstrated that the previously forecast gap is eliminated following a more favourable funding settlement, updated financial assumptions and continued prudent financial management. The Council has subsequently approved a balanced 2026-27 budget, no longer forecasts a funding gap over the planning period, and is making planned contributions to reserves rather than relying on reserve depletion to balance future budgets.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report for Quarter 1 and Rolling Audit Plan Proposal for Quarters 3 & 4
findings.headline: Heads of Internal Audit and Counter Fraud remain in interim arrangements without permanent appointment.
findings.detail: While the council reports no vacancies in the Internal Audit team overall, the posts of Head of Internal Audit and Head of Counter Fraud remain filled by interim arrangements rather than permanent appointments. This follows recruitment of a new trainee auditor and counter fraud assistant, but signals that these key governance leadership roles have not been permanently filled.
findings.matters: Persistent interim arrangements in senior governance posts may signal recruitment difficulty or delayed decision-making; lenders assess management stability and capability in assessing credit risk.
findings.figures: 2 key governance posts in interim arrangements
findings.quote: Interim arrangements for the Head of Internal Audit and the Head of Counter Fraud remain in place.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report for Quarter 1 and Rolling Audit Plan Proposal for Quarters 3 & 4
findings.headline: Contaminated land function depends on a single officer with no formal quality assurance, peer review or conflict of interest controls.
findings.detail: The audit of the council's statutory contaminated land service (Environmental Protection Act 1990) found documented procedures and risk-based assessment processes but identified significant control gaps: no formal quality assurance, no peer review arrangements, and roles/responsibilities not formally documented. The council notes the service is heavily reliant on one officer, creating oversight and resilience risks.
findings.matters: Single-point-of-failure in a statutory environmental function creates reputational and potential financial liability; lenders assess whether councils have designed controls adequate to statutory duties and material operations.
findings.figures: 2 medium recommendations, 1 low recommendation; service reliant on single officer
findings.quote: The service is heavily reliant on a single officer, creating oversight and resilience risks.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report for Quarter 1 and Rolling Audit Plan Proposal for Quarters 3 & 4
findings.headline: Angel Centre planning permission secured, but funding and governance approvals remain outstanding before construction can commence.
findings.detail: The audit found strong governance and robust financial controls over the Angel Centre capital project. Planning permission, a major project milestone reducing strategic risk, has now been approved. However, the council notes that construction cannot proceed until remaining governance and funding approvals are obtained, meaning the funding solution is not yet finalized.
findings.matters: Capital project delivery and financing are core to assessing council financial sustainability; approvals still required means committed spend and final funding source remain unconfirmed.
findings.figures: Planning permission approved; funding and governance approvals outstanding
findings.quote: Since completion of audit fieldwork, planning permission for the Angel Centre development has been approved. This represents a significant project milestone, reducing one of the project's principal strategic risks and enabling progression towards the next phase of delivery, subject to the remaining governance and funding approvals required before construction commences.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 - Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report for Quarter 1 and Rolling Audit Plan Proposal for Quarters 3 & 4
findings.headline: Risk management framework lacks defined risk appetite and tolerance levels, forcing reliance on informal management judgement.
findings.detail: The audit found that while the council has a risk management framework aligned to good practice, it does not define risk appetite or tolerance levels and provides limited guidance on horizon scanning. Operational risk registers remain incompletely implemented across services. The audit raised five medium-priority recommendations requiring action, indicating inconsistent risk escalation and management decision-making.
findings.matters: Weak governance frameworks in risk management undermine the foundation of financial control; lenders assess whether councils have structured processes for identifying and managing financial and strategic risks.
findings.figures: 5 medium recommendations, 1 low recommendation
findings.quote: The framework does not define the Council's risk appetite or tolerance levels, resulting in a reliance on management judgement when determining acceptable levels of risk and escalation requirements.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Angel Centre capital project flagged in value-for-money findings for weak Member reporting on borrowing and affordability
findings.detail: The auditor's value-for-money findings include commentary on the Angel Centre capital project with a recommendation to strengthen Member reporting on funding, affordability and borrowing implications for major capital projects. This indicates governance gaps in how elected members are informed of the project's cost and financing risks.
findings.matters: Lenders care about whether councils have clear governance and member visibility of major capital project costs and borrowing implications. Weak reporting structures suggest decisions on large capital schemes may not be fully informed by affordability analysis.

findings.quote: Our value for money findings, reported in the 2025-26 Auditor's Annual Report, make commentary on the Angel Centre project and includes one improvement recommendation to strengthen Member reporting in respect of funding, affordability and borrowing implications for major capital projects.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Housing benefit control weakness: £206k of prior-year expenditure misprovided in current year due to failed year-end accruals process
findings.detail: Housing benefit expenditure of £206k relating to 2024-25 was incorrectly recognised in 2025-26 because the year-end accruals process did not catch a backdated April payment that finance was not notified related to the prior year. Testing also identified £357.4k of housing benefit overpayment recoveries classified as income rather than reduction of expenditure, showing inconsistency with stated accounting policy. Auditors made a recommendation to strengthen year-end procedures specifically for housing benefit and other material funding streams.
findings.matters: Control gaps in housing benefit—a material expenditure stream—can lead to misstated liabilities and reserves. The issues show that practice is not aligned with stated accounting policy, raising questions about whether other significant transactions are correctly cut-off.
findings.figures: £206k prior-year expense in current year; £357.4k population of misclassified transactions
findings.quote: We identified Housing Benefit expenditure of £0.206m that related to the 2024-25 financial year but was recognised in 2025-26. Whilst the amount is not material to the financial statements and therefore did not require amendment, it indicates that the Authority's year-end expenditure cut-off and accruals processes did not identify all items requiring recognition in the correct accounting period.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Gross expenditure contracted by £6.033m (9.78%) to £55.613m, forcing auditor to revise materiality downward
findings.detail: Expenditure fell from £61.646m to £55.613m year-on-year. The scale of this decline was material enough that auditors revised their materiality assessment from £1.541m to £1.390m to reflect the lower expenditure base. The audit findings do not explain the drivers of this substantial reduction.
findings.matters: Material contraction in expenditure scale affects the authority's financial footprint, borrowing capacity and service delivery. Substantial year-on-year reductions warrant scrutiny of their underlying causes.
findings.figures: £61.646m prior year, £55.613m current year; £6.033m decrease (9.78%); materiality revised from £1.541m to £1.390m
findings.quote: Draft accounts report gross expenditure of £55.613m, compared to £61.646m in the prior year. This represents a decrease in gross expenditure of £6.033m (9.78%), which we consider sufficiently significant to warrant revision of materiality.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation announced: council to merge with three neighbours into West Kent unitary authority from summer 2026
findings.detail: The Secretary of State announced on 16 July 2026 the decision for Kent's local government reorganisation. Tonbridge and Malling will form a West Kent unitary authority with Maidstone, Sevenoaks and Tonbridge Wells. The audit specifically assessed whether reserves were being run down ahead of merger—a known risk where authorities might deplete balances to offset legacy deficits—and found no evidence of this. Auditors flagged governance and due process as paramount through the transition.
findings.matters: Fundamental structural change affects governance, service delivery, organisational structure and long-term financial planning. Lenders need to understand transition risks and whether the authority is making prudent decisions in its remaining autonomous period.
findings.figures: 16 July 2026
findings.quote: The decision for Kent was announced by the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government on 16 July 2026, with Tonbridge and Malling Borough Council planned to form a West Kent unitary authority with Maidstone Borough Council, Sevenoaks District Council, and Tonbridge Wells Borough Council.

findings.headline: Multi-asset and property fund investments show ongoing unrealised capital losses despite some recovery.
findings.detail: Multi-asset diversified income funds show unrealised capital loss of £351,320 at 31 March 2026, an improvement from £517,950 at 31 March 2025. Property funds (LAPF) also show capital loss positions. Structural changes in managed investment portfolios and increased financial market volatility since 2024 are creating persistent pressure.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - TMBC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Property fund investments crystallized £673,670 in capital losses during 2025/26 from forced disinvestments.
findings.detail: Lothbury Property Trust was wound up with a £582,020 loss. Hermes Property Fund merger on 15 August 2025 triggered involuntary disinvestment with a £91,650 loss. Both exits were outside the council's control, with fund managers not prioritizing smaller investors' positions.

findings.paper_title: Blue Budget Book 2627
findings.headline: General Revenue Reserve declining from £12.3m (2026/27) to £4.6m (2035/36), approaching the £2m minimum floor.
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy projects the General Revenue Reserve will decline steadily from £12,338k at the end of 2026/27 to £4,619k by 2035/36. The council's stated objective is to 'retain a minimum of £3.0m in the General Revenue Reserve by the end of the strategy period and not to fall below £2.0m at any time during the 10-year period'. The projection shows headroom of only £2.6m above the absolute minimum by year 10, with the reserve declining in most years.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's buffer against unexpected costs, service failures, or income shortfalls. A reserve that declines to near-minimum over the planning period leaves the council with little capacity to absorb adverse variations and may force service cuts if assumptions slip.
findings.figures: Reserves 2026/27: £12,338k; Reserves 2035/36: £4,619k; Minimum threshold: £2,000k; Target at end of strategy: £3,000k
findings.quote: To retain a minimum of £3.0m in the General Revenue Reserve by the end of the strategy period and not to fall below £2.0m at any time during the 10-year period.

findings.paper_title: Blue Budget Book 2627
findings.headline: External auditor identified a procurement weakness in internal control arrangements; improvement plans being monitored.
findings.detail: Following the 2024/25 audit, Grant Thornton concluded the authority has 'proper arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources'. However, one weakness 'in arrangements covering Procurement remains and improvement plans are now in place and are being monitored'. This is the only control weakness flagged in the audit conclusion, indicating a specific governance gap in how the council manages supplier spend and procurement discipline.
findings.matters: Procurement weakness is a common source of cost overrun, fraud, or wasteful spend in local authorities. For a lender, an auditor-flagged weakness in this area suggests elevated risk of overspending or poor value on major projects (including the Angel Centre).
findings.figures: One weakness identified; no financial impact quantified
findings.quote: Following the 2024/25 audit, our external auditor (Grant Thornton UK LLP) concluded the Authority has put in place proper arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. One weakness in arrangements covering Procurement remains and improvement plans are now in place and are being monitored.

findings.paper_title: Blue Budget Book 2627
findings.headline: Kent Business Rates Pool dissolving from end of 2025/26, removing pooling gains as a future income source.
findings.detail: The council participated in the Kent Business Rates Pool, which generated gains through the pooling mechanism. The pool is dissolving at the end of 2025/26 due to 'changes in baseline levels and risks surrounding growth in rateable values'. The document states this 'does not preclude the reformation in later years subject to Government approval', signalling that pooling gains can no longer be relied upon and future reformation is uncertain.
findings.matters: Loss of an intermittent but valuable income source (the 2025/26 budget shows pool gains of £428,688) removes flexibility. Combined with the baseline reset that absorbed all prior growth, this leaves the council with no upside from local business rate performance.
findings.quote: Due to the changes in baseline levels and risks surrounding growth in rateable values from 2026/27 the Kent Business Rates Pool to the decision to dissolve the pool from the end of the 2025/26 Financial Year. This does not preclude the reformation in later years subject to Government approval.

findings.paper_title: Blue Budget Book 2627
findings.headline: Government grant funding falls £866,000 by 2028/29 due to Fair Funding Review and Business Rates Reset absorbing all prior growth.
findings.detail: The council's grant settlement declined £100,247 in 2026/27 (1.1% cut). Over the three-year settlement period to 2028/29, the council receives £866,000 less than the 2025/26 baseline. This reflects deliberate policy: the Fair Funding Review rolled together multiple grants and reset business rates baselines, explicitly absorbing all previous business rate growth that the council had accumulated. The document notes this was the 'second largest reduction in Core Spending Power' among all councils.
findings.matters: Structural government funding declines are a key indicator of financial stress for local authorities. This council faces an unusually large cut that persists into future years, reducing financial flexibility at a time when social pressures (homelessness) are growing.
findings.figures: £9,062,754 grant settlement 2026/27 (down from £9,163,001 in 2025/26); £866,000 reduction by 2028/29; Business rates down from £5,324,504 to £3,362,707 (36.8% fall)
findings.quote: the Council will receive £866,000 less in 2028/29 when compared to the notional amount for 2025/26. These amounts could also be subject to alteration in 2027/28 to take account of changes in the Councils Rateable Value of Business Rate premises on 31st March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Blue Budget Book 2627
findings.headline: Angel Centre leisure replacement project costs £19.4 million with final approval deferred to Autumn 2026.
findings.detail: The council is planning a major replacement leisure centre at an estimated cost of £19.4m based on RIBA Stage 2 completion. Funding is to come from a combination of council reserves, external borrowing, and contributions from the Leisure Trust and developers. The final decision on whether the project will proceed has been deferred to Autumn 2026, creating material uncertainty over a capital commitment representing 77% of the council's estimated total capital spending over the next two years (2026/27-2027/28: £1.4m + £15m).
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial stability needs to understand whether this project will proceed and on what borrowing terms. If it proceeds, it materially affects the council's debt position and affordability; if deferred, it signals reconsideration of a long-standing commitment.
findings.figures: £19.4 million estimated cost (RIBA Stage 2), £1.4m budgeted 2026/27, £15m budgeted 2027/28, £3m budgeted 2028/29
findings.quote: A major project is underway to replace the existing Angel Leisure Centre with a new, state-of-the-art Leisure Centre located on the Sovereign Way Mid Car Park. The estimated cost of the project is currently around £19.4 million, based on the completion of RIBA Stage 2. Funding for the development is expected to come from a combination of sources, including funds held by the Council, external borrowing, and external contributions from the Leisure Trust and developer funding. A final decision on whether the project will proceed will be made by Full Council in Autumn 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: Angel Centre replacement is a material capital commitment still in development without finalised business case or funding
findings.detail: The Angel Centre replacement has been agreed in principle but officers have not finalised the business case or funding arrangements. The Capital Strategy includes intentions to earmark funds to support development costs, but final project approval remains pending.
findings.matters: Major capital schemes without final business case or funding plan represent contingent exposure; scope or cost changes mid-delivery can force reserve drawdown or borrowing decisions
findings.figures: Annual capital allowance £500k until 2027/28; specific project funding unquantified pending finalisation
findings.quote: Whilst the replacement to the Angel Centre in Tonbridge has been agreed in principle, officers are yet to finalise the business case and funding arrangements for the final project approval by Members.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: The balanced position depends entirely on three specific savings of £800k that council flags as fragile assumptions
findings.detail: The nil funding gap relies on: office accommodation scaling-back (£200k), increased council-owned temporary accommodation use (£200k), and leisure trust net service fee (£400k). The S25 explicitly states 'a number of factors assumed in future years could be different and therefore the funding gap may reappear', directly flagging these assumptions carry material risk.
findings.matters: A balanced budget with no contingency is weaker than one with headroom; if any major saving fails, the council moves to deficit with limited options
findings.figures: £200k office scaling; £200k homelessness service reduction; £400k leisure income; £895k central government funding reduction by 2028/29
findings.quote: This nil position assumes that some long term reductions in cost or increased income will occur in the MTFS, namely the scaling back on office accommodation in the sum of £200,000, the increased usage of Council owned or leased temporary accommodation for Homelessness clients of £200,000 and a net income from the service fee from the Leisure Trust of £400,000... a number of factors assumed in future years could be different and therefore the funding gap may reappear.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: Refuse, recycling and street cleansing contract recommissioning could force rebudget and gap reassessment if costs exceed assumptions
findings.detail: The budget is built on assumed costs for refuse and street cleansing services. However, the contract recommissioning process has not concluded — results are expected after the budget is set. An adverse settlement could flip the council from balanced to deficit within weeks, requiring a further Cabinet report.
findings.matters: Refuse collection is a major fixed cost; an adverse contract can rapidly consume headroom and force reserves or borrowing decisions mid-year
findings.figures: Results expected after 2026/27 budget-setting; timing creates the risk window
findings.quote: There are further risks arising from the recommissioning of the refuse, recycling and street cleansing contract, the results of which are expected after this budget will be set, meaning that the funding gap may require reassessment early in the new financial year, with a further report being presented to Cabinet.

findings.paper_title: Annex 16a Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves Statement 2627
findings.headline: Homelessness accommodation costs have risen significantly and managing them may require reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council has experienced recent significant cost increases for temporary accommodation for homelessness clients. The MTFS plans to control these through providing council-owned and managed accommodation, but explicitly flags that this 'could require some reserve funding depending on the time taken to achieve these goals'. This creates operational stress in a statutory service and contingent reserve exposure.
findings.matters: Unexpected reserve drawdowns to fund statutory homelessness provision signal underlying service stress and reduce financial flexibility for other demands or shocks
findings.figures: Recent significant increases in costs; council-owned accommodation solution timeline uncertain
findings.quote: In terms of homelessness, the MTFS assumes that the recent significant increases in costs will be brought under control over the medium term through the provision of council owned and managed accommodation, the achievement of which could require some reserve funding depending on the time taken to achieve these goals.

findings.paper_title: 01.05 Capital Strategy Annex 5 2026-27
findings.headline: Medium-term capital funding gap: borrowing may be needed beyond 2027/28
findings.detail: The annual capital allowance has been uplifted to £500,000 through 2027/28 to account for Local Government Reorganisation, up from £250,000. The council's financial projections acknowledge that once this uplift ends, borrowing may be necessary to fund capital schemes. This indicates structural capital funding pressure even before Angel Centre repayments would begin.
findings.matters: Signals that capital investment is resource-constrained and borrowing is part of the council's medium-term financial planning, not a one-off decision.
findings.figures: Capital allowance uplift: £250,000 to £500,000 through end of 2027/28; uplift ends 2027/28
findings.quote: Based on the agreed capital plan and future projections the Council may need to borrow to fund such expenditure beyond 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: 01.05 Capital Strategy Annex 5 2026-27
findings.headline: Angel Centre replacement project (£19.4m) will require borrowing
findings.detail: The council approved a £19.4 million capital scheme for Angel Centre replacement at Full Council on 8 April 2025. The Capital Strategy confirms that borrowing will be necessary to finance part of this project. This represents the council's first material borrowing, as it currently holds no debt (nil outstanding at 31 March 2025). The council is seeking alternative financing to reduce the borrowing requirement, but the shortfall is expected.
findings.matters: A £19.4m debt commitment is material and changes the council's capital structure from no leverage. Lenders need to understand the project business case, repayment profile, and whether the revenue base can support debt service alongside existing spending.
findings.figures: £19.4 million capital cost; Debt Outstanding at 31 March 2025: Nil
findings.quote: it is likely that borrowing will be necessary in order to provide some of the financing for the project

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Service area cost pressures across homelessness, leisure trust utilities, and waste continuing to require careful management
findings.detail: The council flags ongoing cost pressures in multiple service areas including leisure trust, utility costs, waste, and homelessness. These are described as being managed carefully but remain areas requiring active oversight. Homelessness is flagged separately with sustained demand and increased temporary accommodation costs, partially offset by £1.6m Local Authority Housing Fund and new owned/leased accommodation portfolio development.
findings.matters: These ongoing operational pressures eat into the £600k savings target. If any of these services deteriorate faster than anticipated, the first-tranche deadline becomes harder to meet.
findings.figures: £1.6m Local Authority Housing Fund received for temporary accommodation portfolio
findings.quote: Leisure Trust Utility costs Waste, Homelessness and Local Plan continue to be service areas of financial pressure and are being managed carefully.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Angel Leisure Centre replacement will require borrowing, reports due early 2025/26
findings.detail: The council has decided it needs to plan for potential borrowing for the replacement of Angel Leisure Centre. This is a capital commitment of unspecified value, with reports on the borrowing requirement expected in the first part of 2025/26. This represents a material fixed obligation beyond the operational savings challenge.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess total debt capacity and the timing of this borrowing against the operational deficit challenge. Angel Centre is a revenue-generating asset (trust-operated) so replacement affects both capital position and leisure trust sustainability.
findings.figures: Angel Leisure Centre replacement borrowing requirement; reports due first part 2025/26
findings.quote: Council will need to plan for potential for borrowing in relation to replacement of Angel Leisure Centre. Reports due to come to Members in first part of 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1a - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: £2.8m medium-term funding gap with £600k first tranche due 1 April 2026
findings.detail: The council anticipates a £2.8m funding gap over the next 4-5 years following national Funding Reform. The immediate challenge is delivering £600k of savings by April 2026, but only £300k has been identified so far. A new savings programme is being devised by Management Team with details to be reported to Cabinet.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see whether this council can execute identified savings on schedule. Only 50% of the first tranche is identified with less than 6 months to deliver.
findings.figures: £2.8m funding gap over 4-5 years; £600k first tranche by 1 April 2026; £300k identified and reported September 2025
findings.quote: expected funding gap to be £2.8m. This can be broken down into tranches over next 4 to 5 years with first tranche of £600k to be achieved by 1 April 2026. £300k has now been identified and reported to both Cabinet and FRPSSC in September 2025

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Fixed Asset Register update from prior year remains in progress; only land and buildings reviewed to date
findings.detail: A recommendation from the 2023-24 audit to update the Fixed Asset Register is still open and in progress. Land and buildings FAR was reviewed in 2022-23 but other asset class registers remain to be reviewed. This multi-year control improvement has not progressed beyond the initial phase, suggesting resource or priority constraints.
findings.matters: Asset register completeness is fundamental to accurate financial reporting and capital asset management. Slow progress on prior-year control improvements suggests implementation challenges that could affect the council's ability to remediate other control findings.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Work remains in progress. Recommendation remains open.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Bank reconciliation control weakness: unreconciled trivial balance not investigated timely throughout the year
findings.detail: The audit identified an unreconciled trivial balance in the cash account (Collection Deposit Book) and a cumulative running difference that was not investigated or resolved promptly during the year. The council attributes this to staff illness and a system upgrade. Although immaterial, this indicates a control weakness in a fundamental control. Management agrees to prioritise resolving all reconciling items timely.
findings.matters: Bank reconciliation is a key control for financial governance. Control weaknesses, even on immaterial amounts, suggest potential gaps in the control environment and cash management resilience that affect risk assessment.
findings.figures: Balance is trivial (below £74,500 reporting threshold)
findings.quote: During our review of cash and cash equivalents, we identified an unreconciled trivial balance in the cash account, which represents the Council's Collection Deposit Book. Furthermore, there has been a cumulative running difference throughout the year that was not investigated or reconciled in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Pension liability fell by £3.245m, from £6.127m to £2.882m, reducing long-term financial risk
findings.detail: The council's defined benefit pension liability improved substantially. The pension fund is now in surplus, with fund assets of £106.4m against defined benefit obligations of £97.7m. The auditor found no issues with the valuation and confirmed the judgments were appropriate. This is a material improvement in the council's financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a primary long-term financial commitment for councils. A £3.245m reduction improves the council's balance sheet and borrowing capacity, reducing financial risk for lenders and improving the council's flexibility.
findings.figures: Pension liability fell from £6.127m at 31 March 2024 to £2.882m at 31 March 2025. Fund assets £106.4m vs defined benefit obligations £97.7m.
findings.quote: The pension fund net liability is £2.882m in the Council's Balance Sheet at 31 March 2025, falling by £3.245m from £6.127m at 31 March 2024

findings.paper_title: 01 Report of Head of Finance and s151 Officer
findings.headline: Business rates income forecast £60,282 below estimate due to empty properties and delayed property valuations
findings.detail: Predicted net business rates income is £4,149,489 against the original estimate of £4,209,769. The shortfall is driven by increased levels of empty business properties and awaited valuations of business properties adjacent to Junction 5 of the M20. The valuations are described as 'awaited', indicating uncertainty.
findings.matters: Material headwind in business rates—a key revenue stream—reflecting economic weakness in the commercial property market. Valuations pending for properties that may represent significant income once confirmed.

findings.paper_title: 01 Report of Head of Finance and s151 Officer
findings.headline: £2.8m medium-term funding gap has only £302,500 identified from first £600,000 saving tranche, with further savings not yet quantified
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies a £2.8m funding gap requiring £600,000 savings across four tranches by February 2026 budget setting. From base budget reviews, the council has identified £182,500; adding a £120,000 inflation underbid on waste contracts brings the total to £302,500, just meeting a £300k milestone. However, the council is now in discussions with service directors on additional savings which are described as 'currently being collated' and to be discussed in November budget processes.
findings.matters: Only 50% of first-tranche savings identified through straightforward base budget reviews; gap-closing plan depends on an inflation windfall; additional savings remain unquantified and behind schedule entering the critical budget-setting period.
findings.figures: £2.8m total funding gap; £600,000 first-tranche target; £182,500 identified from base reviews; £120,000 inflation underbid; £302,500 total; £300,000 milestone
findings.quote: The MTFS agreed in February 2025 had a funding gap of £2.8m, this target was broken down into 4 tranches £600k to be achieved by the time the budget is set in February 2026 for the 2026/27 Budget.

findings.paper_title: 01 Report of Head of Finance and s151 Officer
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend forecast to reach £180,000 by year-end if client numbers do not improve
findings.detail: Client numbers stand at 122 at end of July (down from 129 in May) against a budgeted target of 120 by year-end. Current overspend against the profiled budget is £60,000; if client numbers and placements do not change, this will grow to an estimated £180,000 full-year overspend. The report notes this was also highlighted in the prior year.
findings.matters: Material overspend in a specific service indicates either a forecasting error or genuine service delivery challenge. The council says efforts continue to reduce numbers, but progress so far is insufficient.
findings.figures: 122 clients at end July, 129 in May, 120 budgeted; £60,000 current overspend, £180,000 forecast full-year
findings.quote: As at the end of July, there is an overspend against profiled budget of circa £60,000 and therefore if the current client numbers and placements were not to change the predicted overspend against the original budget by year end would be £180,000.

news_drafts.headline: Tonbridge and Malling eliminates £2.8m funding gap but LGR pause creates 2026-27 uncertainty
news_drafts.lead: The council has eliminated a previously forecast £2.8m funding gap and moved to a balanced budget for 2026-27, following a favourable government funding settlement and updated financial assumptions. The auditor confirmed the accounts are sound with no significant weaknesses. However, uncertainty has grown after government paused local government reorganisation decisions on 7 September. The council had been planning to merge with Maidstone, Sevenoaks and Tonbridge Wells into a West Kent unitary authority, but the vesting date is now uncertain. The auditor flagged the pause as creating heightened risks to financial stewardship during 2026-27.
